items.prose: Over 200 trading days, 40 had a volume spike and 80 were down days. 30 days had both.
items.question: What is $P(\text{spike} \mid \text{down})$? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of a spike given a down day

feedback.correct: 30 of the 80 down days had a spike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the down days, then count the spikes among them.

byKey.inverse: That is $P(\text{down} \mid \text{spike}) = \tfrac{30}{40}$, the condition turned around.
byKey.all: You divided by all 200 days. Only the 80 down days are left.

explain.text: Given a down day, the group is the 80 down days, and 30 had a spike: 0.375. Turned around, $P(\text{down} \mid \text{spike}) = \tfrac{30}{40} = 0.75$. Same overlap, different groups.

items.prose: A surveillance alert flags 98% of insider trades and 2% of ordinary trades. Only 0.5% of trades are insider trades.
items.question: A trade is flagged. What is the chance it is an insider trade? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of insider trading given a flag

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two paths that end in a flag.

byKey.inverse: That is the chance an insider trade is flagged. Turn it around with the base rate.
byKey.base: That is the base rate. The flag should raise it.
byKey.joint: That is insider and flagged together. Divide by every flag.

explain.text: Insider and flagged: $0.005 \times 0.98 = 0.0049$. Ordinary and flagged: $0.995 \times 0.02 = 0.0199$. So about 80% of flags are false, because insider trades are rare.

items.prose: Picture 10,000 loan applications, 400 of them fraudulent. A check flags 75% of fraudulent applications and 5% of genuine ones.
items.question: How many applications are flagged in all?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply each rate inside its own group, then add.

byKey.everyone: You took 5% of all 10,000. The 5% applies to the 9,600 genuine applications: 480.
byKey.fraud: You counted only flagged fraud. Add the 480 genuine applications flagged.
byKey.genuine: You counted only the false flags. Add the 300 fraudulent applications flagged.

explain.text: 75% of 400 is 300 and 5% of 9,600 is 480, so 780 are flagged. Only $\tfrac{300}{780} \approx 0.38$ of them are fraud.

items.prose: A signal fires on 45% of up days and 15% of down days.
items.question: What is the signal's likelihood ratio for an up day?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the firing rate on up days by the rate on down days.

byKey.diff: You subtracted the rates. A likelihood ratio divides them.
byKey.flip: You divided the down-day rate by the up-day rate. Put the hypothesis you are testing on top.

explain.text: A firing is 3 times likelier on an up day than on a down day, so each firing multiplies the odds of up by 3.

items.prose: You give a bond a 25% chance of an upgrade. A rating-agency comment is 4 times likelier before an upgrade than otherwise.
items.question: What is your new probability of an upgrade? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert to odds, multiply by 4, then convert back.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.25 by 4. Multiply the odds instead.
byKey.lr-odds: You took 4 to 1 as the new odds. The ratio multiplies the old odds of 1 to 3.
byKey.prior: That is where you started. The comment should move you.

explain.text: 25% is odds of $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Times 4 gives $\tfrac{4}{3}$, so $p = \tfrac{4}{7} \approx 0.57$.

items.prose: You start at 10% that a stock is in a takeover battle. Two independent news signals arrive, each with likelihood ratio 3.
items.question: What is your probability after both? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 3 twice.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.1 by 9. Multiply the odds instead.
byKey.one: That is after one signal. The second multiplies the odds by 3 again.
byKey.added: You added the ratios to get 6. Independent ratios multiply, giving 9.

explain.text: Odds start at $\tfrac{1}{9}$. Two ratios of 3 multiply them by 9, to odds of 1, which is a probability of 0.5.

items.prose: A coin is drawn from a jar. It is fair with chance 0.5, lands heads 75% of the time with chance 0.25, or has two heads with chance 0.25. It is flipped twice: two heads.
items.question: What is the chance it is the two-headed coin? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each prior by the chance of two heads, then normalise.

byKey.lik-norm: You normalised the likelihoods without the priors. The fair coin is twice as common, so weight by the priors.
byKey.raw: That is the product for the two-headed coin. Divide by the total of all three products.
byKey.one-flip: That uses one flip. Two heads have likelihoods $0.25$, $0.5625$ and $1$.

explain.text: Two heads: fair $0.5 \times 0.25 = 0.125$, biased $0.25 \times 0.5625 \approx 0.1406$, two-headed $0.25 \times 1 = 0.25$. The total is 0.515625, so the two-headed coin has $\tfrac{16}{33} \approx 0.485$.

items.prose: Events $A$ and $B$ both have positive probability.
items.question: Which expression equals $P(B \mid A)$?

options.why: That is the condition turned around. The two are equal only when $P(A) = P(B)$.
You swapped $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. The bottom must be the probability of the condition, $A$.
That is $P(A \cap B)$. Divide it by $P(A)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $P(A \cap B)$ two ways and divide by $P(A)$.

explain.text: $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)$. Divide by $P(A)$ to get $P(B \mid A)$.

items.prose: In a pool, half the stocks are overvalued. A screen flags 70% of overvalued stocks and 10% of the rest.
items.question: A stock is flagged. What is the chance it is overvalued? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the two flagged paths.

byKey.hit: That is the screen's hit rate. Turn it around.
byKey.base: That is the chance before the screen.
byKey.joint: That is overvalued and flagged together. Divide by every flag, 0.4.

explain.text: $0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.35$ and $0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.05$, so $0.35 / 0.4 = 0.875$. With an even base rate it reduces to $\tfrac{0.7}{0.7 + 0.1}$.
